Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Women receiving omega-3 plus vitamin D co-supplementation had a greater reduction in depression than the placebo group.
Sentence: "There was also a significant difference between the group receiving both supplements and the group receiving only placebos in terms of reduction in depression and stress (p < .05)."
Measured as: depression (Depression Anxiety Stress Scale-21)
Population: 168 reproductive-aged women with pre-diabetes and hypovitaminosis D
Intervention: omega-3 (two 1000-mg tablets daily) plus vitamin D (50,000 IU every 2 weeks) for 8 weeks
Comparator: placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 168
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: There was no difference in depressive symptom scores (CES-D) between the 50,000 IU and 5,000 IU vitamin D3 dose groups.
Sentence: "There was no difference in CES-D scores by treatment dose."
Measured as: CES-D scores
Population: Women with type 2 diabetes, significant depressive symptoms (CES-D) and low vitamin D
Intervention: Vitamin D3 50,000 IU weekly orally for 6 months
Comparator: Active comparator vitamin D3 5,000 IU weekly
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 129
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

content.text: {"rationale":"Study A compares omega-3 plus vitamin D against placebo and finds benefit, while Study B compares high-dose against low-dose vitamin D and finds no difference, so the comparators differ in kind.","verdict":"genuine","reason":"comparator","also_differs":["intervention","population","outcome_measure"],"detail":"comparator: placebo vs 5,000 IU weekly vitamin D3 active control; A also adds omega-3, 8 weeks vs 6 months, DASS-21 vs CES-D"}
